HTML5 officially recognizes over 2,000 named character references (entities), covering a vast range of symbols, mathematical operators, and special characters. However, many of these are not maintained or consistently supported across all browsers or rendering engines, often requiring developers to fall back to Unicode decimal or hexadecimal codes to ensure proper display.

Key Issues with Unmaintained HTML Entities

  • Limited Browser Support: While roughly 250 entities are widely supported, many of the 2,000+ HTML5 entities are not in all system fonts or supported by MathJax, forcing browsers to rely on available system fonts.
  • Case Sensitivity and Semicolons: HTML entities are case-sensitive (e.g., Á vs á). While legacy HTML allowed omitting semicolons for certain entities, modern HTML5 parser rules require them, and omitting them can result in parsing errors.
  • Broken Rendering: If an entity is not recognized by the browser, it may render the raw text (e.g., &fake;) instead of the intended character.
  • Symbol Gaps: Certain ranges of characters may not exist, or fonts may lack the necessary glyphs

Q: Avoiding race conditions with file creation/modification in bash A:

Anything that creates a lock will do. Another solution:

echo $$ >> lockfile
locked_by=$(head -1 lockfile)
if [ $$ = "$locked_by" ] ; then
    # My PID locked the files and I can do with it what I want. Not
    # only create, but also edit if I like
    rm lockfile
else
    # Someone else has the file 
fi

Where noclobber works best for creating the file, this works quite well for other actions as well. The echo $$ >> lockfile is sufficiently atomic.
